title: Why Maya buried tiny ceramic spoons
topic: Why the ancient Maya buried their dead with tiny ceramic “spoons” (Mesoamerica, 600‑900 CE)

lines: A priest steadies a handful of tiny ceramic spoons over a fresh burial.
The clay cups glint like tiny moons in the dim light.
He whispers that each spoon carries a secret for the dead.
His apprentices laugh, saying the dead don’t need kitchen tools.
One scoffs, "What will a ghost eat?"
Another rolls his eyes, shaking his head.
The priest places each spoon beside the skull, the clay cool against the earth.
He slides a red powder into every tiny bowl.
The air smells faintly of metal and incense.
You see how you tuck a favorite trinket into a loved one’s pocket for comfort.
It feels like a promise that something familiar travels with them.
The real reason: the spoons held cinnabar, a bright red mercury sulfide.
Cinnabar was used in Maya funerary rites to feed the spirit’s journey.
Its vivid colour symbolized blood, life, and the after‑world.
Because cinnabar is toxic, those tiny spoons turned every grave into a silent, centuries‑long warning.
Even centuries later, the poison still lingers in the soil.

claims.claim: The Classic Period Maya used cinnabar (HgS) in decorative and ceremonial, including funerary, contexts.
Cinnabar was placed in burial contexts, suggesting it was a ritual offering to the dead.
